LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.question: How do you estimate token cost for a conversation?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.reference_answer: Tokens are the units the model reads and produces. They are not identical to words: punctuation and pieces of a word can each become tokens. At runtime I account separately for the system instruction, chat history, retrieved policy snippets, tool arguments and the model answer. Too many input tokens increase cost and can slow prefill, while an overly small output limit truncates answers. For a voice assistant I keep context focused so the user receives a grounded answer with low latency.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.technical_context: A model-specific tokenizer maps text to token IDs. Prompt, retrieved context, tool schemas, tool results and generated answers contribute to different portions of token usage. Character count and word count are only approximations. Budget output tokens and preserve room for the system prompt, conversation and retrieved evidence.
common_mistakes: Assuming one word equals one token
Treating a context window as free memory
Omitting tool and retrieval tokens from budgeting
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.project_context: In the banking voice assistant, policy chunks plus speech transcript and tool results compete for the context and affect response delay and billing.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.question: Why are transformers useful for language models?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.reference_answer: A Transformer is the architecture behind many language models. First text becomes tokens and vector representations. Attention lets each token use relevant previous context, while feed-forward layers transform those representations. A decoder-only model applies causal masking and predicts one next token at a time. During serving, the prompt is prefetched and generated tokens are decoded using a KV cache. In my Azure voice-agent work I use the hosted model rather than training it, so the important design choices are context quality, token usage and latency.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.technical_context: An input is tokenized and embedded with position information, then processed through stacked attention and feed-forward layers. In decoder-only LLMs causal masking prevents attending to future tokens. Layer normalization and residual paths stabilize training. During inference prefill processes prompt tokens and decode generates new tokens autoregressively.
common_mistakes: Calling attention a database search
Claiming a decoder sees future output tokens
Confusing inference orchestration with model training
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.project_context: The banking voice assistant uses a hosted GPT model in Azure AI Foundry, so you orchestrate inference and monitor latency; do not claim you trained its Transformer.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.question: What does attention do in a transformer?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.reference_answer: Self-attention allows each token to combine information from other relevant tokens. The model creates query, key and value vectors; query–key similarity determines weights and the weighted values form a contextual representation. Multiple heads capture different patterns, while decoder models mask future tokens. Longer prompts require more attention work, which matters for voice response latency. We manage this at the application level by retrieving concise policy evidence and limiting unnecessary history, not by claiming to modify the hosted model architecture.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.technical_context: For each head, projection matrices form queries Q, keys K and values V. Scaled dot-product attention computes softmax(QKᵀ/sqrt(d_k))V, with causal masks in decoder-only models. Multiple heads learn different relationships. Standard full attention scales quadratically in sequence length for score computation, though optimized kernels and attention variants change practical costs.
common_mistakes: Calling attention a simple keyword match
Ignoring causal masks
Assuming every token contributes equally
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.project_context: When explaining Azure-hosted LLM latency, connect longer retrieved policy context to attention/prefill cost; the application does not directly tune attention heads.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.question: Why not use a chat model for similarity search?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.reference_answer: I use embeddings to represent the semantic meaning of questions and document passages as fixed-size numerical vectors. We compare these vectors to find candidates in a knowledge base. The generative LLM does a different job: it reads selected evidence and predicts a response token by token. An embedding alone cannot explain a policy, check an account balance or guarantee truth. This distinction helps design a clear retrieval stage followed by authorized generation or tool execution.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.technical_context: An encoder maps text to dense features for nearest-neighbor search. A decoder LLM predicts sequential tokens from context. Both use learned representations, but storing an embedding does not store a validated answer or execute reasoning.
common_mistakes: Calling embeddings answers
Believing vectors enforce ACL
Treating similarity as reasoning
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.project_context: Your banking voice assistant uses embeddings for policy retrieval and the Foundry LLM to compose the response.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.question: What happens when the context becomes too large?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.reference_answer: The context window is the bounded set of tokens available to the model for one inference. A larger window lets us include more history or documents, but that does not make the model a database. For our banking assistant I keep a compact summary of prior turns, then retrieve only the relevant policy chunks for the new question. I reserve tokens for system instructions and the answer and validate citations separately. This reduces latency and makes it easier to inspect what evidence the model actually saw.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.technical_context: It includes system and developer instructions, prior messages, retrieved chunks, tool outputs and input portions of any modality as counted by the model. The output allocation may share or interact with model limits. Long context is not persistent memory or a guarantee of effective retrieval; older evidence can be forgotten or diluted in a crowded prompt.
common_mistakes: Treating a thread identifier as unlimited model memory
Sending whole documents into the prompt
Ignoring effective retrieval quality
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Model m.project_context: Your assistant can maintain a thread ID while using a bounded conversation summary and current policy evidence to answer a banking question.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.question: What is the difference between inference and fine-tuning?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.reference_answer: Training is the phase where a model learns by changing its weights, typically using gradient descent over data. Inference uses fixed weights to process a prompt and generate an answer token by token. In a production RAG system, we can update policy documents, search indexes and prompts without retraining the LLM. In our banking voice assistant, we use an Azure-hosted model for inference and focus on grounding, tool access and response latency.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.technical_context: Training involves dataset batches, loss gradients and optimizer updates, often on accelerators. Inference tokenizes a prompt, runs model forward passes and autoregressive decoding with sampling and KV caches; tool/RAG data usually changes context, not weights.
common_mistakes: Calling knowledge-base updates training
Assuming inference always requires storing new weights
Ignoring retrieval cost
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.project_context: Your Azure AI Foundry banking assistant orchestrates model inference and retrieval rather than fine-tuning or pretraining the hosted model.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.question: Why can the first message take longer?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.reference_answer: TTFT is the time until the model starts returning its answer, whereas end-to-end latency includes all work until the user receives the result. In a voice assistant, the user also waits for speech endpointing, transcription, retrieval, tool calls and text-to-speech. I would attach a call ID to traces and measure p50 and p95 for each stage. Then I optimize the actual bottleneck: concise retrieval for prefill, streaming output for perceived responsiveness, or a faster tool path when backend calls dominate.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.technical_context: Instrument request ingress, retrieval, reranking, model queue, prompt prefill, first token, generation, tool calls and TTS separately. End-to-end voice latency also includes STT endpointing and audio playback. A fast TTFT does not imply a fast complete action if tools or generation are slow.
common_mistakes: Reporting model generation alone as user latency
Ignoring p95 tails
Reducing STT silence timeout so much that users are cut off
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.project_context: Your voice agent project has WebSocket audio, STT, a Foundry model, tool routes and TTS—trace every hop with a shared call identifier.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.question: Which phase benefits most from prompt caching?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.reference_answer: In model inference, prefill is where the prompt is processed and attention information is cached; decoding is where the model generates each next token. A long retrieved context increases prefill work and can hurt time to first token, while a lengthy answer increases decode time. For our voice agent, I cut irrelevant policy chunks, measure first-token latency separately and stream verified response segments to text-to-speech as soon as safe.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.technical_context: Prefill builds representations and key/value cache for prompt tokens in parallel. Decode reuses that cache to predict successive tokens under autoregressive dependencies. TTFT includes queueing/prefill and often tool retrieval, while long output affects overall decode time.
common_mistakes: Calling prefill the training phase
Expecting full KV cache reuse for unrelated prompts
Measuring only tokens-per-second
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.project_context: Your voice assistant benefits from concise context and streaming for faster first audible response.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.question: What does KV caching save, and when is it invalidated?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.reference_answer: KV cache stores attention key/value tensors from earlier tokens so the model can decode the next token without recomputing the entire prefix. It reduces generation cost, but does not eliminate first-token prefill time. Long prompts, cold workers or cache eviction may still make first replies slow. For multi-user serving I would monitor cache hit rate, memory pressure and eviction alongside first-token latency, because cached keys and values are valid only for the matching prefix and model context.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.technical_context: During autoregressive decoding, transformer layers cache previously computed attention keys and values. New generated tokens add K/V entries, avoiding recomputation over prefix tokens. KV caching primarily speeds decoding; prompt prefill still processes new input. Cache footprint grows with layers, heads and sequence length, and reuse depends on the inference server/session.
common_mistakes: Confusing KV cache with semantic response caching
Claiming it removes retrieval or prefill latency
Assuming it survives every unrelated request
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.project_context: For a voice assistant, persistent conversation context can raise latency; monitor prompt prefill, decode, memory usage and KV-cache eviction separately.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.question: What input changes reduce cache hits?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.reference_answer: Prompt caching can avoid recomputing supported prompt prefixes when subsequent requests share the same model and exact preceding tokens. I keep stable instructions early and variable customer data separate, then measure actual cache-hit rates and TTFT. I do not assume every Azure model or deployment offers identical caching semantics. Cached computation is not conversation memory, and private tenant information must never be used as a shared authority or leaked through cache design.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.technical_context: Provider implementations and billing vary; reusable static prefixes should be stable while user-private context is appended securely. Cache hits depend on exact tokens and model support; cache entries must never be treated as user authorization or durable model memory.
common_mistakes: Assuming caching stores facts forever
Claiming guaranteed hits
Mixing user-private inputs across tenants
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.project_context: Your bank voice assistant has common instruction prefixes but must not cross-contaminate customer or tenant data.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.question: Can temperature zero guarantee an accurate answer?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.reference_answer: Temperature scales how strongly the model favors high-probability next tokens. Lower values tend to be more predictable; higher values introduce variation. Top-p can restrict the candidate token mass as another sampling control. In banking, I usually use constrained outputs and conservative settings for routing and policy answers, but I still validate factual claims and tool arguments. Zero temperature alone cannot guarantee correct, reproducible or authorized behavior.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.technical_context: Sampling draws from model token probabilities using temperature and optional top-p/other decoding constraints. Setting temperature to zero does not guarantee identical responses in distributed services; factuality must be tested independently.
common_mistakes: Calling temperature a confidence score
Believing zero temperature means zero hallucinations
Using randomness instead of data validation
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.project_context: For your banking tool-routing decisions, prefer constrained schemas and deterministic checks over hoping a low temperature prevents mistakes.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.question: What steps would you take to optimize latency?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.reference_answer: I profile cost and latency stage by stage: STT, retrieval, model prefill, decoding, tools and TTS. Then I remove duplicated conversation history, keep high-value policy evidence and cap verbose answers. I choose model capacity based on actual evaluation results rather than using the largest model for every intent. In a voice assistant, over-compression can harm accuracy, so I monitor grounding, user outcomes, input/output tokens and p95 response time together.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.technical_context: Track input, output and cached tokens separately; trim redundant history, rerank shorter evidence, batch compatible calls and choose a model/deployment for the accuracy target. Optimize p95 end-to-end time, not just raw model time.
common_mistakes: Reducing tokens by removing essential citations
Ignoring retriever/tool charges
Optimizing average latency only
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.project_context: Your Azure voice assistant can reduce TTFT through lean retrieval while avoiding excessive model/tool retry calls.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.question: Why can first response time spike even with a KV cache?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.reference_answer: When the first answer is slow, I inspect a distributed trace before changing the model. I check request queueing, retrieval duration, number of input tokens, prompt cache status and the time to first token. Prefill can dominate for long contexts, while decode dominates a long response. In the bank assistant I would compare traces with compact versus large policy evidence and optimize the demonstrated bottleneck without removing required factual context.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.technical_context: Separate network and queue time from prefill computation, retrieval and tokenization. Compare prompt lengths, cache hits, model TTFT and parallel tool spans. Slow first request can also involve cold start or provider capacity.
common_mistakes: Blaming KV cache for every slow request
Assuming TTFT excludes retrieval
Deleting necessary policy chunks
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Inferen.project_context: In your voice-agent logs, instrument incoming audio, RAG context size, model calls and TTS to identify the actual delay.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.question: What is a dense embedding?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.reference_answer: Dense embeddings encode text into numerical vectors so we can retrieve passages that are similar in meaning rather than only sharing exact words. We generate vectors for policy chunks and also for each user query, then compare them in the vector index. Results should still be filtered by document access rights, effective date and tenant before reaching the LLM. An embedding is not a guarantee of truth, so we evaluate retrieval relevance and validate that the final answer is supported by the authorized source.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.technical_context: An embedding encoder maps text into a fixed-dimensional float vector. Similarity search compares query and document vectors with cosine, inner product or distance. Model choice, dimensionality, vector normalization and language/domain coverage affect retrieval quality. Embeddings approximate related meaning; they do not encrypt or verify facts.
common_mistakes: Assuming embedding vectors are encrypted documents
Mixing incompatible embedding spaces
Searching before tenant filtering
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.project_context: In the banking RAG pipeline, policy chunks are embedded at ingestion and the caller query is embedded with the compatible model at retrieval.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.question: How are binary and floating-point embeddings different?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.reference_answer: Normal text embeddings are usually floating-point vectors, not just strings of zeroes and ones. Quantization can compress them into lower-precision numbers or binary codes, improving storage or search speed. That compression can reduce retrieval accuracy, especially for close policy clauses. I evaluate recall at k and latency on real questions before adopting it, and may rerank candidates using full-precision vectors. I would not claim binary embeddings are automatically better or private.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.technical_context: Float32 vectors are continuous numerical arrays; scalar, product and binary quantization map them to lower-bit representations. Binary signatures may speed approximate candidate search but often require float reranking to preserve recall. Benchmark on domain labels.
common_mistakes: Equating embedding with binary encryption
Ignoring quantization recall loss
Changing representation without index migration
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.project_context: Your banking policy search should test whether compression misses rare product codes or important exception clauses.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.question: Why would you choose cosine similarity?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.reference_answer: Cosine similarity compares vector direction, dot product compares alignment weighted by magnitude, and Euclidean distance measures point-to-point distance. If the embeddings are unit-normalized, their neighbor rankings are closely related, so the metric choice often changes less than the quality of the embeddings and index filters. I would not pick a metric only because it is popular; I would benchmark it on real banking policy questions and check retrieval precision and recall alongside latency.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.technical_context: Cosine similarity is a·b/(||a||||b||) and measures angle. Dot product a·b uses both alignment and magnitude unless inputs are normalized. Euclidean distance sqrt(sum((a_i-b_i)^2)) measures geometric distance. For unit-normalized vectors cosine rankings and dot-product rankings are equivalent, while minimizing squared Euclidean distance is also equivalent for the same normalized vectors.
common_mistakes: Using cosine without checking zero-norm vectors
Comparing similarity scores from different models directly
Confusing distance direction with similarity
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.project_context: For banking FAQ retrieval, compare metrics with a fixed labeled set and match the index metric to the embedding model guidance.

LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.question: Why does semantic search find synonyms?
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.reference_answer: Semantic similarity measures how close two passages are in meaning, often using embeddings and cosine similarity. It lets evaluation credit valid paraphrases instead of matching exact words. However, similarity can be high even when an answer reverses a condition or states the wrong number. For interview grading I would combine similarity with required-concept coverage, factual-error checks and human calibration, particularly for security and banking workflows.
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.technical_context: Embedding cosine or learned semantic metrics can compare reference and candidate answers, but similarity is not entailment: it may miss negation, wrong values and unsupported claims. Use concept and factual checks too.
common_mistakes: Using cosine similarity as correctness
Ignoring negation
Penalizing every paraphrase
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals / Represe.project_context: Your GenAI evaluation could use answer-reference similarity as a diagnostic, never its only technical correctness score.

Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / S.question: Where should stable policy instructions live?
Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / S.reference_answer: I separate instructions by authority. System instructions set overarching behavior, developer instructions specify application rules, and the user message supplies the current task. Retrieved policies can ground an answer but must never override the application rules. In the banking assistant, an instruction can tell the model to request verification, but backend account tools independently verify the caller and the account. That is the essential difference between prompt guidance and enforceable security.
Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / S.technical_context: System and developer messages establish higher-priority boundaries; user content is lower priority. Retrieved documents and tool outputs are untrusted data, not a source of authority. Enforcement for access and side effects must live in code, not prompts.
common_mistakes: Putting access control only in a system prompt
Treating quoted documents as developer instructions
Trusting tool arguments because the model generated them
Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / S.project_context: Your banking assistant should keep tenant boundaries and tool policies in server authorization while using instructions to shape phrasing and task sequence.

Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / Z.question: When are examples better than longer instructions?
Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / Z.reference_answer: I start with zero-shot prompting when the task has an explicit schema and clear wording. If the model repeatedly confuses similar banking intents, I add a small set of representative few-shot examples, including boundary cases. I keep examples separate from user content and then test on a held-out dataset, not just those demonstrations. Few-shot can improve consistency, but it adds token cost and cannot replace validation or permission checks.
Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / Z.technical_context: Few-shot examples can improve output format, terminology and edge-case consistency at the cost of extra prompt tokens. Select diverse, valid demonstrations and separate them from the live user request; examples do not guarantee correctness.
common_mistakes: Testing only on the demonstrations
Assuming more examples always help
Including sensitive account data in example prompts
Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / Z.project_context: For the banking voice agent, a few verified examples could stabilize routing when customer phrasing is ambiguous.

Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / C.question: How do you improve reasoning reliability without displaying internal steps?
Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / C.reference_answer: When a task has multiple dependent steps, I break it into verifiable outputs: identify evidence, perform calculations with tools, check constraints, then present a short explanation. I do not require hidden model reasoning to be displayed. For our anomaly RCA workflow, the response should show the measured runtime, the median and MAD baseline, and linked activity logs. Those artifacts let an interviewer or operator verify the conclusion without trusting an unsupported narrative.
Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / C.technical_context: Reasoning-style prompts are not substitutes for actual evidence. Private internal reasoning need not be exposed; request concise decision criteria, tool outputs and checkable calculations. Evaluate outcome accuracy and reproducibility.
common_mistakes: Treating verbose reasoning as proof of correctness
Exposing unnecessary private reasoning
Using chain-of-thought instead of tools for critical arithmetic
Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / C.project_context: The anomaly RCA assistant can surface supporting activities and calculations rather than displaying model-internal reasoning.

Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / R.question: How do you design a robust system prompt?
Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / R.reference_answer: I define the assistant role and the task, then supply only relevant authorized context with document identifiers. I instruct it to cite evidence and say when the information is missing. In a banking assistant, the tenant and verified customer identity come from the server, not from the user prompt. I also validate sensitive tool calls outside the model. This makes prompt behavior predictable without pretending that prompt text is a security boundary.
Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / R.technical_context: Use bounded system directives, role/objective, source delimiters, allowed data, output schema, explicit abstention and current time/version when relevant. Redact secrets before prompts and test adversarial documents.
common_mistakes: Mixing privileged rules with retrieved text
Adding entire document collections
Using user-supplied tenant ID as authority
Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / R.project_context: Your Azure banking assistant retrieves tenant-scoped FAQs; its prompt must distinguish customer speech from authorized policy excerpts.

Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / R.question: How does a ReAct agent decide when to call a tool?
Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / R.reference_answer: ReAct combines model planning with external observations. The agent chooses a permitted tool, the backend checks its parameters and user authorization, and the observation informs the next decision. The loop ends with a supported answer or a controlled fallback. In banking I put an approval boundary before any appointment creation or account action, and cap retries so a tool failure cannot produce an endless conversation or duplicate side effects.
Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / R.technical_context: A controller exposes only permitted actions, validates tool arguments, bounds loop count/time and captures results. Tool observations are untrusted input. A final answer is produced after sufficient evidence or a safe stop condition.
common_mistakes: Trusting tool output as instruction
Leaving execution loops unbounded
Repeating non-idempotent actions after timeout
Prompt Engineering / Prompt patterns / R.project_context: In the voice assistant, an intent router selects the account or scheduling tool; a bounded controller handles observations and user confirmation.

Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / S.question: Why prefer schema validation over parsing free text?
Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / S.reference_answer: I use constrained structured output when model results drive software. First I define a schema with required keys, allowed intent values and bounds. I parse the output and validate it again on the backend. If validation fails, I return a recoverable error rather than guessing the missing field. A valid JSON object still might contain incorrect facts, so authorization, existence checks and business rules are separate stages before any banking tool call.
Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / S.technical_context: Use supported JSON/schema constraints, validate parsed types and value ranges server-side, reject unexpected fields where needed and handle invalid completions. A schema cannot prove that facts within valid JSON are true.
common_mistakes: Believing parseable JSON is necessarily accurate
Running tool calls before validation
Ignoring unexpected enum values
Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / S.project_context: Your voice-agent tools should validate an appointment request schema and then check ownership and slot availability in the backend.

Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / T.question: How do you prevent user text overriding instructions?
Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / T.reference_answer: I store reusable prompt instructions as versioned templates and inject specific values like the user question and retrieved policies into clearly marked data sections. I avoid string-building security instructions from customer input. Before sending a prompt, I restrict length and check that the retrieved evidence belongs to the customer tenant. Templates improve consistency and testing, but they cannot make untrusted source content safe or replace access control.
Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / T.technical_context: Keep stable instructions immutable, escape or delimit substituted strings, version templates, cap substituted text and treat external snippets as data. Differentiate prompt composition from server-side tool authorization.
common_mistakes: Splicing user content into system instructions
Forgetting template-version logs
Allowing unbounded variables to exceed token budget
Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / T.project_context: Your banking RAG prompt can swap approved policy chunks per tenant while keeping the guardrail instructions consistent.

Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / R.question: What should the assistant do when retrieval fails?
Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / R.reference_answer: I distinguish three cases. When the user lacks permission, I refuse the sensitive action. When reliable evidence is missing, I say I cannot confirm the answer and offer clarification or escalation. When a tool is temporarily unavailable, I return a safe retry path and never invent a successful booking. For our voice assistant, all fallbacks should be short, understandable when spoken aloud and recorded for support without exposing personal data.
Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / R.technical_context: Define policy-driven refusal for unauthorized actions, uncertainty-driven abstention for insufficient evidence and safe recovery for transient service faults. Do not leak raw credentials, account details or internal errors.
common_mistakes: Fabricating a bank balance after tool failure
Exposing backend exceptions
Retrying write actions without idempotency
Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / R.project_context: Your banking voice agent needs fallbacks for uncertain STT, failed policy retrieval, account verification and scheduling timeouts.

Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / P.question: How do you detect prompt regressions?
Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / P.reference_answer: I treat prompts as versioned artifacts. Every change runs against a fixed golden dataset with successful, missing-evidence and malicious requests, using both strict checks and evaluator scores. I track the prompt version with the model, retrieval corpus and tool schema so failures can be reproduced. In our banking use case, a new instruction cannot be shipped just because one example improved; the regression gate must protect critical balance and booking paths.
Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / P.technical_context: Record prompt hash/version, model deployment, retrieval index version and eval dataset IDs in traces. Run deterministic contract checks plus probabilistic golden-set scoring across changes; keep rollback capability.
common_mistakes: Evaluating only a happy path
Treating nondeterministic scores as exact
Losing the previous prompt/index version
Prompt Engineering / Reliable output / P.project_context: For your banking assistant, compare prompt revisions on identical FAQ, verification and booking scenarios in CI.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.question: What can go wrong when you extract a PDF?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.reference_answer: Before RAG chunking, I extract text and document structure from the actual file format. I preserve headings, table context and page identifiers, because a flattened interest-rate table can change the meaning of a policy. I remove repeated headers and noise without discarding important values, then scan and validate the input and attach source/version metadata. Scanned PDFs need a separately approved OCR path. I quality-check extracted text before it reaches embeddings.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.technical_context: Parse PDF/DOCX according to media type, preserve page/table boundaries and headings, normalize whitespace, retain provenance and flag OCR-dependent scans. Put size limits, malware scanning and access checks ahead of indexing.
common_mistakes: Assuming every PDF contains text
Merging table columns incorrectly
Dropping document version identifiers
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.project_context: A banking policy update needs accurate extraction and document version metadata before the RAG index is updated.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.question: Why not embed the whole document as one chunk?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.reference_answer: We chunk documents because a single large embedding loses topical precision and a full policy may exceed prompt budgets. I split by semantic sections with measured overlap, attach metadata and evaluate retrieval on a golden set. The chunk size is tuned using recall, precision and latency rather than a fixed guess. I also preserve section titles, page references and ACL metadata on each chunk so retrieval can cite the original text without mixing sensitive documents across users or indexing obsolete versions.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.technical_context: Chunking determines retrieval granularity. Tune token size and overlap to document structure, embedding limits, recall, precision and answer context budget. Preserve section headers, page references, ACLs and source IDs. Overlap can protect boundary context but causes redundancy and higher index/storage costs.
common_mistakes: Using arbitrary character slicing across tables
Treating overlap as always beneficial
Dropping ACL and version fields
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.project_context: In the banking voice assistant, retrieved FAQ or policy chunks should keep product, tenant and version metadata; otherwise a correct-looking clause can come from the wrong bank policy.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.question: How do you prevent cross-user data leakage in RAG?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.reference_answer: I attach source ID, version, effective dates and tenant or group authorization to each chunk at ingestion. At retrieval time the backend derives the caller permissions from a verified session and applies mandatory filters before ranking. The language model never sees unauthorized documents. This is critical in a banking assistant where a semantically relevant chunk from the wrong tenant is still a data leak, even if the final answer happens to look correct.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.technical_context: Index tenant ID, document ID, version, effective dates, page/section and authorization attributes. Enforce access in backend retrieval filters before content reaches an LLM; never rely only on the model to hide unauthorized chunks.
common_mistakes: Trusting tenant ID from user text
Filtering only after the model sees chunks
Forgetting ACL updates after policy changes
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.project_context: Your multi-tenant banking voice assistant needs both tenant-isolated vector search and backend entitlement checks for account tools.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.question: When do you need to re-embed a collection?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.reference_answer: My embedding pipeline starts with authorized, parsed document text, generates stable chunk identifiers and converts each chunk into a vector using a versioned embedding model. I store the vectors alongside source, tenant and policy metadata. At query time I embed the question with a compatible encoder, search only authorized chunks and pass selected text to the LLM. I monitor failures and reindex after model changes rather than mixing incompatible vector spaces.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.technical_context: Use deterministic source IDs, chunking policy, embedding model/deployment version, dimensions and normalized metadata; batch with retry and rate limits. Re-embed when changed text or encoder version requires it, and use atomic index cutover to avoid mixed spaces.
common_mistakes: Using different incompatible encoders for query and corpus
Omitting version tags
Keeping deleted policy chunks searchable
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.project_context: Your voice assistant uses stored banking policy embeddings; customers’ queries are independently embedded with the compatible query model.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.question: What happens after today's policy document update?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.reference_answer: Incremental RAG ingestion tracks changed or deleted source documents, regenerates their chunks and embeddings, and retires stale index entries. Unlike incremental data engineering loads, we must manage embeddings, document versions and retrieval correctness—not merely load new rows. I compare source hashes or CDC events, support tombstones for removals, invalidate cached answers, and run question-level retrieval checks before swapping the active index. A successful ingestion job alone cannot prove the new policy is retrievable.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.technical_context: Track document IDs, content checksums, version IDs, timestamps and deletions. A change triggers reparse, rechunk and reembedding for affected material; stale chunk IDs are tombstoned, index updates are idempotent, and retrieval uses an atomic version/active flag to avoid mixed policy versions.
common_mistakes: Only appending new vectors and leaving stale policy chunks
Ignoring source deletes
Making unvalidated content immediately searchable
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.project_context: For updated banking policies, a checksum/event pipeline can process the changed document, switch active version only after validation, and quarantine failed ingestions.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.question: How does incremental RAG indexing differ from CDC?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.reference_answer: Data engineering incremental ingestion is usually about copying or merging changed source records into tables. RAG incremental indexing has extra work: identify document versions, re-parse changed pages, regenerate affected chunks and embeddings, and remove stale vectors. The knowledge base must expose only the active authorized version. In a bank policy update, an ADF copy can succeed while RAG still gives an obsolete answer; index freshness and retrieval regression tests close that gap.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.technical_context: CDC/watermarks capture database row changes while RAG detects document deletions, replacements, layout/chunk changes and encoder version changes. RAG must tombstone obsolete chunk IDs and update index metadata in addition to any underlying file pipeline.
common_mistakes: Confusing Delta MERGE with vector reindex
Leaving superseded chunks in search
Not tracking deleted sources
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.project_context: Your ADF/Databricks pipelines handle incremental data ingestion; your banking RAG index needs its own consistency and deletion workflow.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.question: How do you stop answers citing an obsolete policy?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.reference_answer: To prevent stale answers, every chunk carries its source ID, version and effective date. When a document changes, I create the new chunks and embeddings and only then switch the active version. Old chunks are deleted from live search or excluded by mandatory filters. I verify that known obsolete clauses no longer appear in top results. This is different from keeping old source files in audit storage, which can remain accessible only through appropriate historical workflows.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.technical_context: Store source ID/version and chunk lineage; on replacement, build the new chunk set, atomically mark its version active, remove or filter old versions and retain audit references separately. Use effective/expiry dates for policy changes.
common_mistakes: Appending without deleting
Treating indexing success as a consistent cutover
Forgetting effective dates and tenant scope
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Document ing.project_context: Your banking policy RAG layer should identify the applicable effective policy before selecting chunks.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.question: Do we chunk the user question too?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.reference_answer: In a standard RAG flow, yes, the user query is embedded. The document chunks already have vectors in the index. We use a compatible embedding model for the query, retrieve the nearest allowed chunks and optionally rerank them. A normal short question does not need chunking: chunking primarily helps ingest long documents. I also use metadata and tenant filters before retrieval and test whether the top results really contain the policy evidence needed to answer.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.technical_context: At query time, preprocess only as needed, encode with the retrieval embedding model and search the index. The user query usually is not chunked unless it is exceptionally long or composite; query rewriting/decomposition is a separate step. Search must apply authorized filters and may combine keyword retrieval and reranking.
common_mistakes: Assuming queries are never embedded
Chunking every short query
Relying on similarity without document permissions
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.project_context: Your banking voice assistant can embed the transcribed intent question, retrieve permission-filtered FAQs and only then compose the LLM answer.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.question: How do you choose vector storage?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.reference_answer: I choose vector storage by workload rather than popularity. FAISS is useful as a local nearest-neighbor index, pgvector integrates with PostgreSQL data and permissions, and Azure AI Search offers managed lexical, vector and hybrid retrieval features. I evaluate filtering, update frequency, tenant boundaries, latency, cost and operational ownership. In banking, the ability to enforce authorization before retrieval and trace the policy source matters as much as vector similarity quality.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.technical_context: Compare pgvector, FAISS, Azure AI Search and managed vector services across hybrid text/vector search, metadata filters, index types, tenant isolation, update load, observability, backups and cost. FAISS is an index library rather than a full multi-tenant database.
common_mistakes: Calling FAISS a complete secure database
Ignoring hybrid keyword needs
Picking service without update/ACL benchmarks
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.project_context: In your banking assistant, vector choice should support tenant scoping, managed identity and policy document versioning.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.question: Why can dense retrieval miss exact identifiers?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.reference_answer: Dense semantic search converts the user question into an embedding, compares it to stored document vectors and returns top candidates by similarity. It handles paraphrases better than exact matching, but it can miss identifiers and confuse short or negated phrases. For a banking voice agent I use it to find relevant policy clauses, combine it with keyword search when needed and never use nearest-neighbor text as a substitute for account balance retrieval.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.technical_context: Embed compatible queries and chunks; approximate nearest-neighbor index returns candidates by cosine or dot-product. Dense search may miss exact IDs, rare acronyms, negation or very recent names; hybrid lexical retrieval can compensate.
common_mistakes: Treating similarity as evidence of truth
Using dense retrieval for exact account numbers
Ignoring query/document encoder mismatch
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.project_context: Your policy FAQ retrieval can use dense search while balance/account identifiers must go to verified tools.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.question: Where can BM25 outperform vector search?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.reference_answer: BM25 is a keyword-based retrieval algorithm. It scores term overlap, giving more weight to uncommon query words and controlling the effect of long documents. In enterprise RAG it is very useful for exact policy codes and pipeline errors that embeddings may blur. I would combine BM25 with semantic retrieval, apply the same security filters to both and compare results on a labeled question set before choosing fusion weights or a reranker.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.technical_context: BM25 is a bag-of-words lexical ranker based on term frequency saturation, inverse document frequency and length normalization. It excels at exact product names, policy IDs, error codes and rare identifiers, while dense embeddings help with paraphrases. A hybrid retriever merges both candidate lists then may rerank.
common_mistakes: Assuming semantic search always wins
Letting lexical results bypass tenant filters
Treating BM25 score as factual confidence
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.project_context: For the RCA assistant, use lexical matching for pipeline IDs and codes while vector retrieval serves explanatory runbook questions.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.question: When would you use hybrid rather than pure semantic retrieval?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.reference_answer: I use hybrid retrieval when the query mixes exact terms and natural-language meaning. One retriever finds documents by BM25 keyword matches, and another finds semantically similar chunks with embeddings. We combine their results, typically with reciprocal rank fusion, and rerank the best candidates if latency permits. Security and freshness filters must apply to both branches. Finally, I measure context precision and recall with real questions rather than assuming hybrid search is always better.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.technical_context: Run lexical and embedding retrievers over the same authorized candidate scope. Fuse scores using calibrated weights or rank-only methods such as reciprocal rank fusion, then optionally rerank against the whole query. Normalize filters, source version and document identifiers across both indexes, otherwise fusion can surface stale or unauthorized snippets.
common_mistakes: Adding raw lexical/vector scores without calibration
Duplicating the same chunk
Neglecting latency or ACL parity
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.project_context: Your assistant retrieves banking policies and could use BM25 plus embeddings, while the pipeline RCA assistant benefits from exact pipeline ID matching.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.question: How does metadata filtering improve relevance?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.reference_answer: Before ranking policy chunks I apply mandatory tenant and authorization filters, and usually active-version and document-type restrictions. Top-k then controls how many candidates move to reranking and the prompt. A very low k can hide the needed clause; an excessive k adds irrelevant context and latency. I tune both on labeled banking questions, measuring recall and wrong-tenant leakage rather than choosing a universal k like five for every query.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.technical_context: Apply mandatory tenant, ACL and active-version filters as early as supported; tune k and candidate pool on recall@k, precision and latency. Some vector indices approximate filtering, so test whether filters are enforced before answer assembly.
common_mistakes: Accepting tenant filter from user prompt
Believing top-k is a confidence score
Retrieving many chunks without budget checks
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.project_context: Your voice assistant should derive tenant scope from the session, not from a model-generated filter.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.question: How does a reranker differ from a vector index?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.reference_answer: I use reranking after a cheap broad retrieval stage, not on every document in the bank. The initial index finds a candidate set; a semantic reranker uses more query–passage detail to sort them and select the best evidence for the LLM. I measure retrieval quality and extra latency, especially p95, because a voice assistant must respond quickly. I also keep tenant/ACL filters enforced before both stages.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.technical_context: A first-stage lexical/vector search has high recall and low cost; second-stage semantic reranking scores candidate pairs and selects a shorter context. Use metrics such as MRR/nDCG and benchmark added p95 latency.
common_mistakes: Calling reranking an embedding replacement
Reranking unauthorized chunks
Skipping latency benchmarks
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.project_context: Your Azure banking FAQ answers benefit from reranking only when the measurable quality gain offsets voice latency.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.question: What is the difference between RRF and cross-encoder ranking?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.reference_answer: RRF is a fusion method: it combines rank positions from several searches, such as BM25 and vector retrieval, without needing those systems to share a score scale. A cross-encoder is different: it reads the query and each candidate passage jointly and produces a relevance score. I may use RRF to build a diverse candidate list, then cross-encode the top subset. I benchmark extra latency and still apply tenant permissions before retrieval.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.technical_context: RRF assigns rank-based scores across lexical and vector result lists without directly comparing heterogeneous raw similarity scales. A cross-encoder jointly processes query–passage text and is usually costlier but can yield stronger semantic ordering.
common_mistakes: Treating RRF as a trained model
Cross-encoding entire knowledge base
Comparing raw BM25 and cosine scores directly
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Vector & hyb.project_context: Your policy search could fuse Azure AI Search lexical/vector candidates before a constrained reranking stage.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.question: How would you construct a safe RAG prompt?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.reference_answer: After retrieval I filter to authorized active passages, remove duplicates and order them by relevance and source quality. I give each excerpt a citation identifier and keep it clearly separated from trusted instructions. I respect the model token budget and reserve space for a concise answer. For a banking voice assistant, this reduces time to first token and prevents a noisy prompt from burying the key policy while preserving traceable sources.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.technical_context: Reserve token budget, prefer non-duplicated current evidence, carry precise citation IDs and separate source text from instructions. Account for contradictions and recency before response generation; preserve legal/disclaimer requirements.
common_mistakes: Concatenating everything retrieved
Losing citation IDs
Letting a retrieved clause act as an instruction
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.project_context: In your banking voice assistant, the model receives selected tenant-specific policy snippets and the customer question—not all tenant data.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.question: Are citations alone sufficient to prove correctness?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.reference_answer: Citations in RAG should reference real retrieved sources, not names invented by the model. I persist document ID, effective version and chunk location with every retrieval hit. After generation, the application verifies that cited IDs were actually retrieved and authorized for that user. This supports debugging when policy wording changes and helps auditors inspect why an answer was given. A citation does not itself prove the claim, so groundedness evaluation is still necessary.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.technical_context: Store immutable document ID, section/page, effective version, access permissions and chunk offsets with retrieval hits. Require the answer to identify which claims use which authorized passages; validate references server-side where possible. Displaying a plausible-looking citation string generated by an LLM is not proof of support.
common_mistakes: Allowing fabricated document IDs
Citing outdated versions
Revealing inaccessible document titles
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.project_context: Your banking voice assistant can keep source IDs in the tool trace even if the spoken reply uses a brief natural-language attribution.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.question: What happens if relevant context cannot be found?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.reference_answer: I treat retrieval failure as an explicit outcome rather than silently sending an empty context to the model. I check whether filters removed everything, whether indexing is stale or whether the search timed out. If there is no valid policy evidence, the assistant says the answer cannot be confirmed and offers clarification or escalation. I capture an anonymized trace so engineers can distinguish an access problem from an information gap. This avoids hallucinated banking advice.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.technical_context: Distinguish no hits, filter exclusions, search timeout, stale index and conflicting evidence; log retrieval trace safely, choose a permitted fallback or escalation and test no-evidence responses in golden sets.
common_mistakes: Inventing facts from model memory
Retrying with tenant filters removed
Hiding search timeouts from monitoring
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.project_context: Your banking voice assistant can offer human escalation or an official channel instead of guessing a policy amount.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.question: When do you use multi-query retrieval?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.reference_answer: I rewrite ambiguous user questions only to improve retrieval, not to alter what was asked. For a loan-closing question, I might search “foreclosure fee” and “early repayment charge” in parallel, merge and deduplicate results, then rerank. I preserve the original wording, negations, dates and verified tenant filters throughout. I measure whether this improves recall without adding irrelevant context or delaying the voice response too much.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.technical_context: Keep original intent and constraints, bound number of rewrites and deduplicate retrieved candidates. Never rewrite away tenant, date, negation or account-type conditions; evaluate recall against a held-out dataset.
common_mistakes: Dropping negation or time qualifier
Hallucinating customer constraints
Producing too many expensive queries
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.project_context: Your voice assistant can normalize ASR wording before policy search while retaining the raw transcript for audit.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.question: Why did you not use Graph RAG in the voice assistant?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.reference_answer: We chose conventional RAG for policy FAQs because document search was sufficient and simpler to maintain. Graph RAG adds entity and relationship traversal for multi-hop questions, but also increases indexing, security and operational complexity. I would benchmark it against a fixed multi-hop question set before adoption. A graph would only be justified if entity relationships repeatedly defeated hybrid retrieval, and each graph edge would need provenance, tenant permissions and refresh logic when source policies changed.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.technical_context: Graph RAG builds or queries entity and relationship structures alongside document retrieval. It helps multi-hop questions and relationship reasoning, but requires entity extraction, graph maintenance, permission-aware traversal and extra latency. Hybrid vector+graph retrieval is often more practical than replacing vector RAG.
common_mistakes: Claiming graph traversal automatically prevents hallucinations
Ignoring edge-level permissions
Using a graph for simple single-policy lookups
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.project_context: Banking FAQ questions mainly need grounded policy retrieval. A graph is justified only when tracing linked accounts, organizational relationships or multiple-hop RCA, and must enforce tenant authorization on every traversal.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.question: When would SQL be better than RAG?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.reference_answer: Not every question belongs in a vector database. For exact account balances, booking slots or pipeline runtimes, I use a permission-checked SQL or API tool that returns current structured records. RAG is useful for explaining policies and unstructured documents. In our banking assistant, I first verify identity, retrieve the balance from the authorized backend and then let the model explain it without changing the number. All queries are parameterized and scoped.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.technical_context: Run parameterized read-only queries through allowlisted tools, derive user scope from verified identity, validate schema/queries and set row/timeout limits. Combine structured tool answers with RAG only when interpretation from policies is needed.
common_mistakes: Asking LLM to guess balances
Letting model generate unrestricted SQL
Treating semantic similarity as exact record retrieval
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Answer gener.project_context: Your bank voice agent uses an account-lookup tool for balances and RAG for product FAQs; no embeddings are required to calculate a balance.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.question: What does context precision measure?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.reference_answer: Context precision measures the usefulness of the retrieved material, especially whether relevant chunks appear near the top. If the model gets lots of unrelated policy paragraphs, it may still write a fluent but wrong or incomplete answer. I create a golden set of questions with relevant source passages and score retrieval separately from generation. Then I inspect failures by policy type and tune chunking, metadata filters, hybrid search or reranking. It helps explain why groundedness alone is not enough.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.technical_context: Ragas-style context precision emphasizes relevant retrieved contexts earlier in a ranking; exact implementation depends on metric variant and reference data. An answer can be faithful to irrelevant passages, so retrieval relevance and groundedness must be evaluated separately. Inspect slices such as short FAQs, multi-hop policies and identifier-based lookups.
common_mistakes: Calling context precision answer accuracy
Ignoring rankings
Changing the golden set while comparing runs
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.project_context: In banking FAQs, label which policy chunks were relevant to each question, then compare retriever and reranker versions with the same golden dataset.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.question: What does low context recall suggest?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.reference_answer: Context recall measures whether the retrieved documents cover the key evidence needed for a correct answer. A system may retrieve one very relevant chunk but miss an exception from another page. In that case precision can look good while recall is weak. I would evaluate the retrieved evidence against reference passages, test larger top-k or query decomposition when needed, and balance recall against added tokens and latency. High-risk banking workflows also require deterministic policy validation.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.technical_context: Recall is the fraction of relevant evidence captured; reference-based or LLM-judged implementations approximate it differently. High top-k precision can coexist with low recall if a critical exception clause is missing. Evaluate chunk boundaries, page-level parsing, multi-query retrieval and relevant document versions.
common_mistakes: Treating recall as number of chunks returned
Increasing top-k without measuring noise
Failing to test policy exceptions
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.project_context: Your banking policy RAG needs recall checks for important exception and customer eligibility conditions before the assistant takes action.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.question: How is faithfulness different from factual accuracy?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.reference_answer: Faithfulness asks whether the answer is supported by the context the system retrieved. A judge can compare each factual claim with that evidence and flag unsupported details. It does not prove that the context itself is correct or current. In a banking assistant, a model can accurately summarize a superseded fee schedule while still giving a wrong answer. So I pair faithfulness with current-version retrieval tests, authorization checks and human review for critical cases.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.technical_context: Decompose response into checkable claims and estimate their entailment from provided passages. A faithful answer can inherit errors from outdated sources; measure source truth and access separately.
common_mistakes: Equating faithfulness with truthfulness
Ignoring stale policy documents
Letting the judge see evidence the generator never saw
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.project_context: Your bank RAG evaluation needs context-faithfulness scoring plus version-validity tests.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.question: Can an answer be faithful but irrelevant?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.reference_answer: Answer relevance measures how directly the reply responds to what the user asked. An answer can be perfectly grounded in policy excerpts yet irrelevant if it talks about the wrong banking product. I evaluate question–answer fit, whether all parts were addressed and whether the answer is sufficiently concise for speech. I score faithfulness and relevance separately, because optimizing citations alone can still leave customers with unanswered questions.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.technical_context: Compare the question to answer intent and coverage; detect tangents and missing requested subparts. Relevance differs from citation faithfulness and readability/coherence.
common_mistakes: Using groundedness as a relevance proxy
Rewarding excessive tangents
Ignoring multi-part requests
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG metrics.project_context: Your voice assistant should judge intent coverage independently of whether a policy quote is supported.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Retrieval &.question: What happens when embeddings change but vectors remain old?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Retrieval &.reference_answer: When changing an embedding model, I would create a new versioned index and re-embed the complete active document corpus. Mixing old and new vectors can break ranking even if their dimensions match. I would test representative questions, retrieval recall, grounded-answer quality, latency and cost against the existing index. After validating access filters and document versions, I would move query traffic to the new index behind a reversible switch. I would retain the old index briefly for rollback and retire it after acceptance.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Retrieval &.technical_context: Vector similarity is meaningful only in a compatible representation space. Even equal embedding dimensions do not guarantee semantic compatibility after switching model versions. Record embedding model, version, preprocessing and dimensions with each indexed chunk. Build a parallel new index, regenerate all active vectors, compare offline recall and latency on a fixed query set, then atomically switch reads. Keep the old index for rollback until validation is complete.
common_mistakes: Mixing vectors from incompatible embedding spaces
Assuming equal dimensions imply interchangeable scores
Forgetting deleted documents or tenant ACLs during reindex
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Retrieval &.project_context: For a banking-policy RAG assistant, propose a versioned embedding namespace and a dual-read evaluation period, rather than claiming an untested migration was already delivered.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Retrieval &.question: Where do you put reranking and how do you measure its cost?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Retrieval &.reference_answer: I would insert reranking after first-stage hybrid or vector retrieval and before assembling the final prompt. The retriever should produce enough candidates to maintain recall, because a reranker cannot find passages we never retrieved. I would compare baseline and reranked results on a labeled question set using recall at k, ranking quality, groundedness and p95 response latency. For a voice assistant I would keep the rerank candidate count small, enforce a time budget and fall back to original retrieval when necessary.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Retrieval &.technical_context: A two-stage retrieval pipeline may use lexical, vector or hybrid search to gather top-k candidates, optionally fuse scores, and apply a cross-encoder or model-based reranker only to that bounded set. A reranker generally improves order among retrieved candidates but cannot recover a relevant passage absent from the candidate set. Measure candidate recall@k before reranking and nDCG/MRR, answer groundedness, token budget, p50/p95 latency and unit cost after reranking. Apply query-class policies and timeouts rather than rerank arbitrarily large lists.
common_mistakes: Calling reranking a replacement for first-stage recall
Measuring only average latency, not tail latency
Reranking passages across tenants without preserving ACL checks
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / Retrieval &.project_context: A banking voice assistant values low conversational latency; evaluate a bounded rerank stage with a fallback to the initial retrieval order if it times out.

RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG lifecycl.question: How do you handle a revised policy without leaving stale snippets?
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG lifecycl.reference_answer: My incremental RAG ingestion would fingerprint every policy document and track source IDs and versions. A changed file is reprocessed into versioned chunks, while deleted or superseded chunks are tombstoned and excluded from search. I would verify counts, permissions and sample questions before exposing the new version. Retries must be idempotent, and the process should reconcile missed deletions. This differs from incremental data movement because the goal is not only moving changes; it is maintaining a consistent retrieval index and citations.
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG lifecycl.technical_context: Give each source document a stable ID, version and content checksum. An ingestion job compares current source manifests against the prior snapshot to detect new, updated and deleted documents. Reparse/rechunk changed versions; write new vectors with source/version metadata; then retire stale chunks or mark a tombstone with a deletion watermark. Respect incremental ingest retries, atomic cutover, ordering, ACL changes and eventual index lag. Queries should select only active document versions, with source citations tied to the exact revision.
common_mistakes: Appending new chunks while retaining obsolete chunks as active
Using only filenames as stable document identities
Deleting all old vectors before validating a replacement index
RAG & Knowledge Retrieval / RAG lifecycl.project_context: For a banking knowledge base, design a change manifest and tombstone reconciliation step; avoid asserting automatic correctness without a post-ingestion retrieval test.

LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.question: When would you choose LangGraph over a simple chain?
LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.reference_answer: LangChain helps connect language models, retrievers and tools. LangGraph is useful when the application needs explicit state and branching: for example an intent router, identity verification, a scheduler tool and a fallback path. I can reuse LangChain integrations inside LangGraph nodes. I choose the simplest workflow that meets the requirement. For a basic document FAQ a chain may be enough, while my banking voice-assistant use case benefits from traceable multi-step decisions and retry handling.
LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.technical_context: LangChain commonly provides prompts, runnable chains and integrations. LangGraph models execution as nodes and edges over typed state, supporting conditional routing, cycle guards, persistence, human approval and resumes. They can be used together: use LangChain components inside LangGraph nodes. A one-step RAG call does not automatically need a graph.
common_mistakes: Treating the frameworks as mutually exclusive
Building a graph for every single prompt
Ignoring durable state and loop limits
LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.project_context: Your banking agent uses a multi-service orchestration pattern where intent routing and tool interactions are easier to inspect as a graph.

LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.question: What does a node return?
LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.reference_answer: In LangGraph, a node is a function or runnable that receives shared graph state and returns changes to that state. A node might classify intent, retrieve policy passages or validate a tool result. Edges decide which node runs next, including conditional routing. I design nodes with clear inputs and outputs so I can test each independently and trace failures. In a banking voice assistant, sensitive actions run only through authorized backend tool nodes.
LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.technical_context: Graph nodes take current state and return partial updates; routing depends on edges rather than calling the next node directly. Pure deterministic nodes are simpler to test than nodes that hide tool side effects.
common_mistakes: Mutating shared state unpredictably
Hiding all work inside one giant node
Assuming every node is an LLM call
LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.project_context: Your banking assistant can separate transcript handling, intent routing, policy retrieval and secure tool calls into nodes.

LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.question: How does routing based on user intent work?
LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.reference_answer: In LangGraph, nodes perform work and edges define the flow. Conditional edges select paths based on the state, while the shared state passes messages and validated tool results across nodes. We use checkpointers when conversations must resume, and guard loops with limits to avoid runaway agent execution. For an approval-sensitive banking tool, the conditional edge can stop at a human confirmation node instead of executing a write. I version state transitions to prevent resumed retries from duplicating operations.
LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.technical_context: Nodes are functions that read/return updates to typed shared state. Edges connect nodes, conditional edges route based on state or classifications, START defines entry, END defines termination. Checkpointers persist graph execution state and thread identifiers associate resumable conversations; looping needs iteration guards.
common_mistakes: Putting authorization only in the router prompt
Mutating hidden globals rather than shared state
Omitting terminal/error edges
LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.project_context: The banking voice assistant routes recognized speech to a policy Q&A path or verified account/appointment tool, then sends a final answer to TTS.

LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.question: What state would a bank assistant keep?
LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.reference_answer: LangGraph state is a typed object shared across execution steps. Each node reads the current values and returns updates such as the detected intent, verified customer ID, retrieved policy IDs or tool result. Conditional edges can then route based on explicit fields instead of guessing from free-form text. For banking, I do not trust a model-generated `verified` flag as authorization; the backend identity check must set it. LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.question: When does an agent stop calling tools?
LangChain & LangGraph / Core graph build.reference_answer: START is the entry point of a LangGraph execution and END represents a terminal step. A graph can end after producing a normal answer, after a clarification request, or after a safe refusal. In an agent that calls tools, I define explicit stop conditions and loop budgets so transient failures cannot run forever. Ending a turn does not have to delete thread state; the next caller utterance can resume with a valid session context.

Allowing infinite conditional cycles
Treating tool timeout as success

LangChain & LangGraph / Runtime design /.question: Why not let an LLM modify database rows directly?
LangChain & LangGraph / Runtime design /.reference_answer: The agent may suggest a tool call, but the tool node controls execution. I validate its parameters, verify the caller identity and check resource access before contacting the banking backend. I also set timeouts and idempotency safeguards and return a structured success or failure observation. For example, balance lookup is an authorized read; appointment booking is a side effect that requires confirmation. This separation stops prompt output from becoming unrestricted database access.

Retrying writes without deduplication
Returning raw internal error messages

LangChain & LangGraph / Runtime design /.reference_answer: In LangGraph, checkpointing records the graph state at execution boundaries and lets a workflow resume, which is useful for multi-turn tasks and human approvals. We associate the persisted state with a stable, user-owned thread ID. For banking I would protect the checkpoint storage with user access controls, avoid storing unnecessary account secrets and track external side effects separately. For example, resuming after an appointment tool timeout must not accidentally create a second booking; that requires an idempotent backend tool.

It supports replays, interruptions and durable state across process restarts, but storage authorization and PII retention must be designed explicitly. Storing raw secrets in state
Assuming checkpoint replay undoes a booking

LangChain & LangGraph / Runtime design /.question: How do you maintain continuity during a call?
LangChain & LangGraph / Runtime design /.reference_answer: Thread-based memory lets an agent remember the conversation over multiple turns. I assign a unique session and thread to each call and persist a bounded state such as verified customer, pending task and previous tool result. On the next utterance, I recover the correct state with server-side ownership checks. I do not put unlimited history into every prompt, nor do I use the thread ID as a substitute for verifying the caller.
LangChain & LangGraph / Runtime design /.technical_context: Use a server-owned unguessable session/thread identifier, checkpoint only necessary state, apply TTL and tenant/user scoping, and avoid storing raw sensitive transcript indefinitely. Never equate a client-provided thread ID with authorization.

Storing sensitive data without retention limits
Trusting client-provided thread as proof of identity

LangChain & LangGraph / Runtime design /.question: Which bank operations require user confirmation?
LangChain & LangGraph / Runtime design /.reference_answer: Human-in-the-loop is a controlled pause, not simply telling the model to be careful. The graph prepares an action, records what will happen and interrupts before any side effect. After the user or authorized reviewer confirms, the backend rechecks the identity and current conditions and only then executes. In banking, I would confirm appointment details and escalate unusual or sensitive transactions. Durable checkpoints prevent the pending task from disappearing between messages.
LangChain & LangGraph / Runtime design /.technical_context: Interrupt graph before irreversible actions; capture exact proposed operation and approver identity, preserve state with durable checkpoint and revalidate permissions, parameters and conditions on resume.

Executing before confirmation
Resuming with stale authorization
